                   Staff’s Final Recommendation on Reliability Standard Assessment and
                   CONE Assumptions


On January 15, 2026, ERCOT filed its initial modeling assumptions for the triennial reliability
standard assessment and a proposal to update the Cost of New Entry (CONE) value. 1
Seventeen interested parties provided written feedback on these assumptions, including the
Independent Market Monitor. 2 On March 23, 2026, ERCOT filed its final assumptions,
incorporating feedback provided by the interested parties. 3

Staff generally agrees with the assumptions that ERCOT included in their final
recommendation. Staff provides this memo to highlight assumptions where Staff’s view

Cost of New Entry (CONE)

CONE for the 2026 Reliability Standard Assessment

Staff agrees with the ERCOT recommendation to update the CONE value that will be used in
this reliability standard assessment. While the CONE value was updated as recently as 2024,
it is important to have a CONE value that accurately captures the expected cost to build a new
generation facility. This value can, in turn, be compared against the market revenues a new
generation facility would be expected to earn within our energy-only market to inform the
Commission’s decision about what market design changes, if any, are needed to incentivize
the level of investment necessary to achieve the Commission’s reliability standard.

Staff also agrees with ERCOT’s recommendation to use a small frame combustion turbine as
the reference technology. That is consistent with previous CONE studies performed for the
ERCOT region, so the estimated costs and expected revenues for a new generation facility
would be more straightforward to understand. Staff acknowledges that gas turbines are not
expected to be widely available until 2030 or later, and this could raise questions about whether
the CONE value used for this reliability standard assessment should be based on a technology
that is not readily available. However, Staff does not believe that current conditions warrant a
change in approach. The inclusion of an updated CONE in the reliability standard assessment
is to determine whether the market design is expected to produce the necessary price signal to
incentivize sufficient generation in the long run. An assessment of the ERCOT energy-only
market and any potential market design changes should not be based on short-term, abnormal
conditions. Instead, it should assume that, in the long-run, things will stabilize, and conditions
will return to normal until such time that sufficient evidence exists to indicate otherwise.
Recent legislation 5 has also emphasized the importance of building thermal dispatchable
generation in the ERCOT region, so the CONE used in the reliability standard of the ERCOT
region should reflect that.

Additionally, Staff recommends that if any generation facilities included an application to
amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity use the frame combustion turbine, ERCOT
and Brattle should consider that information in the update as informative data points to
benchmark.

Lastly, Staff believes that there would be limited value in exploring alternative reference
technologies at this time, and therefore, recommends that the Commission should not direct
ERCOT and Brattle to move forward on that component.

Future Work on CONE

Some interested parties recommended that the updated CONE study explicitly address issues
that were raised by stakeholders and the Commission during the 2024 CONE study. 6 Staff also
raised concerns during the 2024 CONE study, recommending that the Commission retain a
frame combustion turbine as the reference technology absent a deeper dive into the revenues
in excess of operating costs that alternative technologies would be expected to receive. 7 While
Staff does not believe there is sufficient time to address all these concerns for the 2026
reliability standard assessment, Staff does view these and other issues related to CONE as
important for designing our market to achieve the desired reliability outcomes on a long-term
basis. Therefore, Staff recommends that the Commission commit to conducting a full CONE
study in 2028 so that updated information will be available for the 2029 reliability standard
assessment.

Staff Recommendation: The Commission should direct ERCOT to conduct a limited update on
the CONE value, continuing to use the frame combustion turbine as the selected reference
technology. The updated CONE value should be reported in real dollars, not nominal. The
review should include information from any frame combustion turbines included in recent
Commission approved CCN amendments. The Commission should also direct Staff to plan to
conduct a full CONE study in 2028 to better understand and consider a broader selection of
reference technologies, and the expected market revenues each would receive, ahead of the
2029 reliability standard assessment.

Reliability Standard Assessment Modeling Assumptions

Resource Mix [ERCOT Assumption 1.1]

In their initial set of assumptions, ERCOT proposed to use the December 2025 Capacity,
Demand, and Reserves (CDR) Report to establish the generation portfolios for the assessment
for Year 2026 and Year 2029.

Interested parties generally supported this approach in their comments as reasonable for the
Year 2026 assessment. However, many parties expressed concern with applying this approach
to the Year 2029 assessment, stating that the December 2025 CDR Report would not provide
an accurate representation of the Year 2029 resource portfolio. Some recommendations from
parties included:
    • All projects being developed under the Texas Energy Fund should be included.
            o Some parties requested that projects that withdrew their Texas Energy Fund
                applications but indicated that they would continue developing their projects
                should also be included. 8

    •   ERCOT should analyze the annual pace of additions, including resource type, and use
        the additions and resource mix in the current resource trends to forecast the projected
        additions by 2029. 9
    •   The retirement assumptions in the CDR may be overly aggressive and should be
        revisited or considered as a sensitivity. 10
    •   Additional generation capacity should be included in the Year 2029 assessment to
        account for the increased investment incentives as the reserve margins decline. 11
In their final set of assumptions, ERCOT modified the generation included in the Year 2029
portfolio to include Texas Energy Fund projects that qualify to be in the draft of the May 2026
CDR Report, as well as any other significant resource changes. 12

Staff acknowledges that ERCOT’s modified approach for the Year 2029 portfolio is a step in
the right direction; however, Staff recommends that any Texas Energy Fund In-ERCOT Loan
project or Completion Bonus Grant project with a signed loan or grant agreement should be
included, even if it has not satisfied all requirements necessary to be included in the CDR.
There is a high degree of certainty that these plants will be online prior to 2029. At this time,
Staff does not recommend including generation that has withdrawn from the Texas Energy
Fund but indicated that they plan to continue to move forward, nor do we believe that ERCOT
should create a last-minute process to project what new generation facilities might be online
prior to 2029. Staff recommends that ERCOT investigate alternative approaches to identifying
new generation beyond what is counted in the CDR to include in the three-year forward year
for future reliability standard assessments.

Staff Recommendation: The generation mix should incorporate Texas Energy Fund projects
with executed loan or grant agreements, even those that are not currently included in the CDR.
The Commission should also direct ERCOT to investigate alternative approaches for
identifying what generation should be included in the expected system configuration for the
three-year forward year in future reliability standard assessments.

provided in the Energy Information Administration’s (EIA) Annual Energy Outlook, resulting

Almost every interested party that weighed in on the fuel prices recommended that ERCOT
conduct some type of sensitivity analysis on this assumption, including those that supported
ERCOT’s proposed prices. Fuel price assumptions can have a considerable impact on the
modeling results through their influence on factors such as unit dispatch and market prices. 13
Recommended sensitivities included using a range of price outcomes 14 and using other sources
for fuel prices, such as the NYMEX natural gas futures, as an alternative benchmark. 15 Several
parties stated that ERCOT’s proposed fuel prices were too low, with some noting that the EIA’s
Annual Energy Outlook has exhibited meaningful variance from actual market outcomes. 16
Opposing parties recommended that ERCOT use alternative sources to establish the fuel prices
used in the model.

Staff believes that ERCOT’s recommendation to use fuel price assumptions based on the EIA’s
Annual Energy Outlook is reasonable. However, staff also agrees with comments suggesting
that a sensitivity based on an alternative source makes sense. We recommend that this
sensitivity use the NYMEX natural gas futures price for 2029, as this would provide a different
snapshot that could capture how fuel prices impact dispatch and market outcomes.

Staff Recommendation: ERCOT’s proposed fuel price recommendations are sufficient for the
base case, but they should conduct a sensitivity for the Year 2029 based on the NYMEX natural
gas futures as an alternative benchmark.

Load Forecast [ERCOT Assumption 2.1]

ERCOT’s filing outlining their initial assumptions highlighted a potential consideration on
whether the load forecast used in the reliability standard assessment should be based on the
2026 RTP-compliant load forecast that was pending Commission approval. ERCOT noted that
using this forecast would likely result in a delay in beginning the reliability standard
assessment work, as they anticipated that they would have the load forecast developed under
such a compliance plan ready in April or May. 17 Staff included a question to gather the
perspective of interested parties on this issue.

Interested parties nearly unanimously supported ERCOT using the 2026 RTP-compliant load
forecast, even if it prompted a schedule delay. While supportive, a few parties raised concerns

incorporating expectations for transmission development and the batch study process. 19

Staff agrees that ERCOT should develop the 2026 RTP-compliant load forecast and use that
in the 2026 reliability standard assessment. Staff acknowledges the concerns from parties
wanting to ensure any associated delays do not compress the comment windows for interested
parties to file comments with the Commission. Additionally, due to the wide range in potential
load outcomes, ERCOT has proposed to simulate multiple load forecast scenarios with various
Large Load levels, curtailment assumptions, etc.

Staff Recommendation: ERCOT should use the 2026 RTP-compliant load forecast for the 2026
reliability standard assessment, even if it causes a schedule delay. The reliability standard
assessment schedule should be revised to ensure that feedback windows for interested parties
to file comments are not truncated. ERCOT should conduct sensitivities around the large load
forecast and curtailment assumptions. In addition, ERCOT should make the details and results
of these scenarios available to stakeholders. In addition, Staff recommends ERCOT file in this
project the results of large load forecast submitted for the years 2026-2029 as soon as
practicable so the Commission can weigh how much delay will be caused until data is verified
and if ERCOT will be requiring any adjustments per TAC 25.370(e)(2)(B). This will help Staff
to revise the future timelines.

Weather Year Weighting [ERCOT Assumption 2.4]

In a change from previous practice, ERCOT proposed to give heavier weight to weather years
that occurred more recently. 20 Historically, ERCOT has modeled all historical weather years
as having equal probability. Given the amount of interest expressed by parties around the
weighting of weather years during the Commission’s reliability standard rulemaking, Staff
included a question on this topic for interested parties to weigh in on.

While a few parties were supportive, most parties that weighed in did not support ERCOT’s
proposed alternative weighting approach. The following are some of the parties’
recommendations:
    • Weighting approach should be based on a meteorologist or climatologist informed
       methodology. 21

    •     Use multiple approaches, including equally weighting the most recent 15 years and
          equally weighting all 44 years. 22
    •     Weighting for extreme weather years should be reconsidered, with comments focusing
          on the weighting of 2021 and Winter Storm Uri. 23
    •     If ERCOT opts to use a heavier weighting for more recent weather years, weather data
          for 2024 and 2025 should be included as well. 24
Staff appreciates ERCOT’s work in developing an alternative weather year weighting
approach. However, Staff does not believe a methodology that weighs weather years solely on
how recently they occurred is sufficient, nor is there sufficient time to incorporate a new
weighting methodology into the 2026 reliability standard assessment. Therefore, Staff
recommends that ERCOT continue to use the equal weather year weighting approach
employed in previous work and the Commission direct ERCOT to explore improved
methodologies in this area ahead of the 2029 reliability standard assessment.

Staff Recommendation: ERCOT’s default weather year weighting should give each weather
year equal weighting. Improved methodologies in this area are worth exploring, and ERCOT
and interested parties should work towards developing those ahead of the 2029 reliability
standard assessment.

Transmission Representation [ERCOT Assumption 3.1]

ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling capability
in the Strategic Energy Risk Valuation Model (SERVM) software to assess resource adequacy
on a zonal basis that would account for transmission constraints between defined transmission
zones. In their initial SERVM assumptions filing, ERCOT made it clear that any results from
this analysis would be purely informational and not used to determine compliance with the
reliability standard.

There were some parties that supported the inclusion of this additional analysis, with one
pointing to the consideration of zonal and local constraints. 25 Some parties did not oppose the
inclusion of a zonal analysis, but they wanted to make it clear that the results would be purely
informational. 26 There were also several parties that opposed the inclusion of a zonal reliability
study, even if the results would be purely informational. Some of these parties expressed

Staff appreciates ERCOT’s work in this area, as zonal and deliverability analysis is an item
that the Commission has expressed interest in previously, including during the project that
adopted the Commission’s reliability standard. 29 However, Staff agrees with the commenters
that stated this element should not be included in the 2026 reliability standard assessment. This
will be the first formal reliability standard assessment conducted in the ERCOT region, and
any analysis or filings made by ERCOT in this project should focus on whether ERCOT is
meeting the system-wide reliability standard. To be clear, Staff does not oppose continued
work in this area by ERCOT and PowerGEM (owner of the SERVM Software) and encourages
further development that may be considered again for the 2029 reliability standard assessment.

Staff Recommendation: ERCOT should not move forward with the zonal analysis within the
2026 reliability standard assessment.

Thermal Resource Unplanned Outage Modeling, Weather-Related [ERCOT Assumption 4.2]

ERCOT proposed multiple modifications to how weather-related, unplanned outages would be
captured in the model. One of the questions Staff posed was related to the assumption on the
effectiveness of weatherization requirements that have been implemented since Winter Storm
Uri in 2021. Previously, these weatherization requirements were estimated to be effective at
preventing 85% of the cold weather-related generation outages. ERCOT proposed applying a
declining weatherization effectiveness curve that would capture an expected decrease in
effectiveness as temperatures get colder. 30

Comments from interested parties expressed a wide range of views on the declining
weatherization effectiveness curve. Several parties supported ERCOT’s proposed approach,
noting that it is reasonable to assume that weatherization strategies will become less effective
during extreme or prolonged conditions 31 and that a single, static value cannot accurately
reflect how weatherization measures perform across extreme winter conditions. 32 Several
parties opposed utilizing the declining effectiveness curve, noting that there is no data

supporting this change 33 and that, in fact, generator performance during recent events such as
Winter Storm Fern shows that weatherization effectiveness might even be higher than 85%. 34

At this time, Staff does not believe there is sufficient justification to deviate from the 85%
weatherization effectiveness that ERCOT has assumed since the weatherization requirements
went into effect after Winter Storm Uri. There is limited historical data since the weatherization
requirements are still relatively new, and as multiple parties highlighted, the proposed
declining effectiveness curve does not align with the actual operational performance during
Winter Storm Fern. However, Staff supports ERCOT’s continued study in this area.
Accounting for increased outages due to extreme cold weather does happen in other regions,35
and as more data on the effectiveness of the Commission’s weatherization requirements
becomes available, this could be considered for future reliability standard assessments.

In addition, 16 TAC §25.55(i) requires ERCOT to study historical weather data across weather
data across the weather zones in the ERCOT footprint and file a report at the Commission at
least once every five years, beginning no later than November 1, 2026. The 2026 report should
provide valuable insight for evaluating weatherization effectiveness. Staff recommends that
the Commission direct ERCOT to file an additional report with updated data no later than
November 1, 2028. This will ensure the most up-to-date data available can be included in
establishing weatherization effectiveness assumptions for the 2029 reliability standard
assessment.

Staff Recommendation: ERCOT should use the 85% weatherization effectiveness that has been
previously used as the base case. In addition, the Commission should direct ERCOT to file an
updated historical weather study no later than November 1, 2028 to ensure the most recent
data is included in establishing the weatherization effectiveness in 2029.

Magnitude Criterion [ERCOT Assumption 7.1]

For the Year 2026 assessment, ERCOT proposed to use the value of 13,988 MW from the
Report on 2026 Reliability Standard Magnitude that they filed at the Commission.36 For the
Year 2029 assessment, ERCOT proposed to scale the 2026 magnitude by the ratio of the 75th
percentile forecast value for 2029 to the 75th percentile forecast value for 2026, resulting in a
magnitude value of 14,509 MW. 37

The question on the magnitude criterion values for the Year 2026 and Year 2029 assessments
received a mixed reaction from interested parties. Some parties supported ERCOT’s proposed

values, stating that updates from the Transmission and Distribution Utilities provide the best
insights in determining what these values should be. 38 Others were concerned with scaling the
2029 value based on the 2026 value, as there could be structural changes in load composition
or transmission topology that could materially affect the grid’s physical limits. 39 Other parties
disagreed with the proposed 2026 and 2029 values, stating that these are based on low-
percentile load forecasts that do not align with system conditions where reliability events are
expected to occur. 40

Staff agrees with ERCOT’s proposal to use the 2026 value filed with the Commission and with
their proposed methodology for scaling this value for 2029. However, Staff recommends that
ERCOT ensure this scaling is applied to the updated load forecast from the 2026 RTP
compliance plan, if the Commission opts to direct ERCOT to use it in the 2026 reliability
standard assessment.

Additionally, several interested parties also requested clarification around what counts as “load
shed” in the context of the magnitude. Specifically, parties sought clarity around the treatment
of curtailable large loads consistent with Senate Bill 6 (89R) (SB 6). Commenters that
addressed this argued that curtailment of these large loads should not be counted as a firm load
shed event or captured in the reliability standard assessment metrics. 41 Staff agrees. The
curtailment of large loads consistent with SB 6 will occur prior to any firm loss of load event,
and therefore, it is not appropriate for the reliability standard assessment to capture this
curtailment within the metrics, including the amount of load shed with the magnitude metric.

Staff Recommendation: ERCOT should use the methodology they have proposed, using the
reported 2026 magnitude value and scaling it up for 2029. ERCOT should ensure that the
value for 2029 aligns with the updated load forecast from the 2026 RTP compliance plan. The
magnitude values should not include the curtailment of any large loads consistent with SB 6,
and ERCOT should review the methodology used for determining the magnitude values, and if
warranted, propose improvements prior to the 2029 reliability standard assessment.

To enable interested parties to review the results of the reliability standard assessment, Staff
recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to publish any non-confidential data,
including both inputs and outputs, from the reliability standard assessment in this Project.

Timeline

Under 16 TAC § 25.508(c)(3), ERCOT must file the results of its assessment with the
Commission,42 and if the assessment shows that any reviewed system fails to meet the
reliability standard, ERCOT must provide the Commission with both a summary explanation
of any identified deficiencies and a menu of proposed recommended market design changes,
including a primary recommendation, to address the identified deficiencies. 43 Staff
recommends that this step be broken into separate parts in order to allow the Commission and
stakeholders ample time to evaluate results before evaluating market changes:
    • Once ERCOT completes its work on the assessment, they will file the results at the
         Commission and report any identified deficiencies.
    • Next, ERCOT should present these results at a meeting of the Technical Advisory
         Committee (TAC) or a TAC sponsored workshop.
    • After this, ERCOT would then file their recommendations for market design changes,
         including their primary recommendation, at the Commission.
This modification to the schedule most likely will further delay the end of the reliability
standard assessment. However, Staff believes that this additional time for ERCOT stakeholders
to review the results will provide valuable feedback and preparation before ERCOT files their
final market design recommendations at the Commission.

Cost of New Entry (CONE)

CONE for the 2026 Reliabilitv Standard Assessment

Staff agrees with the ERCOT recommendation to update the CONE value that will be used in
this reliability standard assessment. While the CONE value was updated as recently as 2024,
it is important to have a CONE value that accurately captures the expected cost to build a new
generation facility. This value can, in turn, be compared against the market revenues a new
generation facility would be expected to earn within our energy-only market to inform the
Commission' s decision about what market design changes, if any, are needed to incentivize
the level of investment necessary to achieve the Commission' s reliability standard.

Staff also agrees with ERCOT' s recommendation to use a small frame combustion turbine as
the reference technology. That is consistent with previous CONE studies performed for the
ERCOT region, so the estimated costs and expected revenues for a new generation facility
would be more straightforward to understand. Staff acknowledges that gas turbines are not
expected to be widely available until 2030 orlater, and this could raise questions about whether
the CONE value used for this reliability standard assessment should be based on a technology
that is not readily available. However, Staff does not believe that current conditions warrant a
change in approach. The inclusion of an updated CONE in the reliability standard assessment
is to determine whether the market design is expected to produce the necessary price signal to
incentivize sufficient generation in the long run. An assessment of the ERCOT energy-only
market and any potential market design changes should not be based on short-term, abnormal
conditions. Instead, it should assume that, in the long-run, things will stabilize, and conditions
will return to normal until such time that sufficient evidence exists to indicate otherwise.
Recent legislation5 has also emphasized the importance of building thermal dispatchable
generation in the ERCOT region, so the CONE used in the reliability standard of the ERCOT
region should reflect that.

Additionally, Staff recommends that if any generation facilities included an application to
amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity use the frame combustion turbine, ERCOT
and Brattle should consider that information in the update as informative data points to
benchmark.

Lastly, Staff believes that there would be limited value in exploring alternative reference
technologies at this time, and therefore, recommends that the Commission should not direct
ERCOT and Brattle to move forward on that component.

Future Work on CONE

Some interested parties recommended that the updated CONE study explicitly address issues
that were raised by stakeholders and the Commission during the 2024 CONE study.6 Staff also
raised concerns during the 2024 CONE study, recommending that the Commission retain a
frame combustion turbine as the reference technology absent a deeper dive into the revenues
in excess of operating costs that alternative technologies would be expected to receive. 7 While
Staff does not believe there is sufficient time to address all these concerns for the 2026
reliability standard assessment, Staff does view these and other issues related to CONE as
important for designing our market to achieve the desired reliability outcomes on a long-term
basis. Therefore, Staff recommends that the Commission commit to conducting a full CONE
study in 2028 so that updated information will be available for the 2029 reliability standard
assessment.

Staff Recommendation: The Commission should direct ERCOT to conduct a limited update on
the CONE value, continuing to use the frame combustion turbine as the selected reference
technology. The updated CONE value should be reported in real dollars, not nominal. The
review should include information from any frame combustion turbines included in recent
Commission approved CCN amendments. The Commission should also direct Sta# to plan to
conduct a full CONE study in 2028 to better understand and consider a broader selection of
reference technologies, and the expected market revenues each would receive, ahead of the
2029 reliability standard assessment.

Timeline

Under 16 TAC § 25.508(c)(3), ERCOT must file the results of its assessment with the
Commission,42 and if the assessment shows that any reviewed system fails to meet the
reliability standard, ERCOT must provide the Commission with both a summary explanation
of any identified deficiencies and a menu of proposed recommended market design changes,
including a primary recommendation, to address the identified deficiencies.43 Staff
recommends that this step be broken into separate parts in order to allow the Commission and
stakeholders ample time to evaluate results before evaluating market changes:
    • Once ERCOT completes its work on the assessment, they will file the results at the
       Commission and report any identified deficiencies.
    •   Next, ERCOT should present these results at a meeting of the Technical Advisory
        Committee (TAC) or a TAC sponsored workshop.
    •   After this, ERCOT would then file their recommendations for market design changes,
        including their primary recommendation, at the Commission.
This modification to the schedule most likely will further delay the end of the reliability
standard assessment. However, Staffbelieves that this additional time for ERCOT stakeholders
to review the results will provide valuable feedback and preparation before ERCOT files their
final market design recommendations at the Commission.
